## Abstract

Tavakoli et al. perform a cross-species in vivo screen to directly test chemicals for enhanced muscle progenitor cell engraftment. Their findings show that a short ex vivo pre-transplantation treatment with specific compounds is beneficial, improving the engraftment of myogenic progenitor cells and improving cell therapy as a treatment option for degenerative muscle disorders.

## INTRODUCTION

Skeletal muscle is subject to mechanical and physiological stresses throughout life and requires ongoing maintenance and repair, including replacement of myonuclei, to sustain its function. The basic structural unit of skeletal muscle is the myofiber, a multinucleated and post-mitotic cell.1 Because myofibers are multinucleated and structurally complex, they cannot replace themselves through traditional cell division.2,3 Instead, the regeneration of injured myofibers is contingent upon the successful fusion of mononucleated muscle progenitors, called myoblasts, into de novo or residual fibers.4

Myoblasts are primarily generated from resident muscle stem cells, called “satellite cells,” which are Pax7+/MyoD−/Myf5− mononuclear, unipotent stem cells.5–10 Satellite cells localize beneath the basal lamina of muscle fibers11 and generally remain mitotically quiescent in intact (uninjured) adult muscle. Satellite cells undergo activation upon muscle damage, initiating both self-renewing and differentiating divisions and producing daughter myoblasts that fuse together to build, and rebuild, new muscle.12 Chronic muscle damage, caused by repeated injury or genetic disorders such as muscular dystrophies, may deplete satellite cells and impair their function, leading to a diminished regenerative response, progressive loss of muscle mass, and reduction of strength and mobility.10,13–15 Transplantation-based studies in animal models have demonstrated the utility of engrafted satellite cells for regenerating diseased muscle.9,16–21 However, challenges in obtaining adequate numbers of satellite cells from adult skeletal muscle and in achieving sufficient efficiencies for engraftment of culture-expanded cells have presented significant barriers to the clinical application of such transplantation approaches.22,23 While recent efforts have certainly advanced our understanding of the molecular features required for efficient satellite cell self-renewal and engraftment, the relative dearth of small molecules capable of enhancing the efficiency of progenitor cell transplantation remains a challenge for realizing the full potential of cell therapy approaches for muscle disease.24–26

To address this challenge, we devised a screening approach that leverages the ability to rapidly and cost-effectively assess the impact of defined chemical compounds on the engraftment efficiency of muscle progenitors in vivo in zebrafish. Potential pro-myogenic effects of compounds identified through this screen were subsequently validated in assays using highly purified mouse muscle satellite cells.6,20,27 The throughput and accessibility of this model allowed us to evaluate 187 compounds sourced from the ICCB Known Bioactives Library, focusing primarily on lipid mediators, a relatively understudied class of biomolecules that can play key roles in enhancing cell migration and promoting regenerative function.28–31 Candidate compounds were added to the cells in vitro, and 4 h later cells were washed and transplanted. This approach sought compounds that had specific effects on muscle engraftment, limiting the effect of the compounds to the donor cells with little if any exposure of the recipient muscle tissue. These efforts identified two small molecules, lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and niflumic acid (NFA), both of which increased the engraftment efficiency and muscle-forming activity of transplanted myogenic progenitors in zebrafish and mice. RNA-sequencing and calcium-ion imaging studies further revealed that both compounds alter the expression patterns of ion transport genes and increase intracellular calcium concentrations, suggesting that the effects of these lipids are mediated via regulation of calcium-dependent second-messenger systems.32 Finally, supporting the potential translational relevance of these compounds, we documented increased rescue of dystrophin deficiency in dystrophic mice and improved physiologic function in dystrophic zebrafish33 after transplantation with NFA-treated or LPA-treated muscle precursors. In summary, the cross-species approach developed in this study has identified inducers of skeletal muscle cell engraftment and suggests potential opportunities for muscle cell therapy as a treatment option for degenerative muscle disorders.

## RESULTS

### Establishing transplantation parameters for zebrafish muscle cells using a limiting dilution assay

Zebrafish myogenic progenitor cells (ZeMPCs) were generated by in vitro culture of blastomeres from mylz2-GFP, mylz2-mCherry, or myf5-GFP;mylz2-mCherry double-transgenic zebrafish embryos by adaptation of published protocols,34 with myf5 serving as a marker of myogenic progenitors and mylz2 serving as a marker of terminally differentiated muscle cells.35 ZeMPCs were transplanted into the flank muscles on both sides of transparent casper zebrafish recipients (Figure 1A). At 7 days post transplantation (dpt), engraftment success was assessed by in vivo fluorescent stereomicroscopy to detect GFP- or mCherry-tagged donor-engrafted myofibers in the recipient fish. Notably, we observed the persistence of donor-engrafted muscle cells in recipient fish for up to 1 year post transplantation (Figures 1B and 1C). The optimal number of transplanted cells for screening was determined by performing an extreme limiting dilution analysis (ELDA)36 for engraftment. ELDA is a powerful technique to measure the number of cells (potent cells) in a given cell population that perform a particular desired effect. ELDA has not been commonly applied to muscle progenitor transplantation experiments but is routinely used to study blood stem cells.37–40 Here, we applied the concepts of ELDA to accurately calculate the number of muscle-engrafting cells (potent cells) within each population of control- or compound-treated donor cells. In this manner, we were able to test the effect of pre-transplantation treatment with specific compounds on muscle engraftment (the desired effect) by donor cells (potent cells). The use of zebrafish as recipients in these efforts was key, as in total the work reported in this study required approximately 14,000 individual recipient animals.

We first used ELDA to calculate the number of potent cells under control conditions. An initial representative study yielded a 100% successful engraftment rate in fish receiving 700 ZeMPCs, and a 30% successful engraftment rate in fish receiving 100-cell transplants (Table S1). Using ELDA software,36 we calculated that 1 out of 272 ZeMPCs produced under these conditions successfully engrafted, with a 95% confidence interval of 1 out of 211–352 in vitro expanded ZeMPCs (Figure 1D). However, we note that the ELDA-determined frequency of engrafting cells varies slightly across different ZeMPC derivations, likely due to subtle fluctuations in the efficiency or expansion of these embryo-derived cells in culture. To account for this, we included independent ELDA assessments for both experimental and control conditions in each subsequent transplantation experiment and always used the same freshly derived ZeMPCs for the different treatment groups within an individual experiment. Throughout these studies, we established a system to perform rapid and cost-effective cell-transplant-based screening in zebrafish, which we subsequently deployed to identify chemical compounds that increase the engraftment efficiency of ZeMPCs in vivo.

### myf5-expressing myogenic progenitors exhibit superior engraftment efficiency

To define the myogenic cell subpopulation(s) that supports high-efficiency engraftment in zebrafish muscle, myf5-GFP;mylz2-mCherry double-transgenic embryos were generated, dissociated, and cultured with basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF). The in vitro expanded muscle cells at day 2 were purified into four distinct populations by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS): myf5-GFP+mylz2-mCherry− cells, myf5-GFP− mylz2-mCherry+ cells, myf5-GFP+mylz2-mCherry+ cells, and myf5-GFP− mylz2-mCherry− cells (Figure 1E). Based on their myogenic marker expression, these sorted cells represent myogenic progenitors, terminally differentiated muscle cells, differentiating myoblasts, and other non-muscle cell types, respectively. Cells from each sorted population were transplanted intramuscularly into ten individual casper recipients at each of three doses: 50 cells, 100 cells, or 250 cells. Fish were anesthetized and imaged at 7 dpt, and the numbers of potent cells (those capable of muscle engraftment) within each of the different donor cell subpopulations were calculated by ELDA (Figure S1A). These data revealed that engrafting cell frequency was significantly higher for myf5-GFP+mylz2-mCherry− cells (1 out of 97.7), confirming the previous studies20,41 showing that myogenic progenitor cells engraft more readily in muscle relative to the other populations evaluated (Figures 1F, 1G, and S1).

### Transplanted embryo-derived zebrafish muscle cells fuse with recipient muscle cells

To determine the manner by which transplanted donor ZeMPCs contribute to muscle regeneration in vivo, whether by de novo myogenesis or fusion with endogenous myocytes, 1 million in vitro generated muscle cells from mylz2-GFP embryos were transplanted into mylz2-mCherry adult fish (Figure 1H) to generate a large patch of engrafted tissue. At 7 dpt, the recipient fish were euthanized and the dissected muscle was fixed, sectioned, stained with DAPI, and prepared for imaging to discriminate donor-derived (GFP+), host-derived (mCherry+), and hybrid (GFP+ and mCherry+) muscle cells. A cross-section of one recipient fish flank shows both mylz2-mCherry-tagged recipient muscle cells and mylz2-GFP-tagged donor cells (Figure 1I). Although the cells at the center of the engrafted region expressed only GFP, cells at the border were marked with both GFP and mCherry (Figure 1I, bottom row), indicating that the transplanted muscle cells are capable of both de novo myogenesis and fusion with recipient’s muscle. To further test the in vivo fusion capacity of transplanted donor cells, we next mixed a limited number of in vitro expanded muscle cells from mylz2-mCherry embryos with an equal number of cells from mylz2-GFP embryos (1:1 ratio; 100 cells per group), similar to the method of Moore et al.41 The cell mixture was transplanted immediately into casper recipients (Figure S2A). At 7 dpt, recipients were euthanized and the dissected muscle was fixed, sectioned, stained with DAPI, and prepared for imaging. A cross-section of the recipient fish flank shows both mylz2-mCherry and mylz2-GFP single-color fibers, as well as double-positive (mylz2-mCherry and mylz2-GFP) hybrid fibers (Figure S2B). In this experiment, single-color fibers were equivalently distributed among GFP+ (47%) and mCherry+ (42%) fibers, with 11% of fibers exhibiting both GFP and mCherry. These data clearly demonstrate the fusogenic ability of transplanted donor cells (Figure S2C). As has been shown previously,41 most fibers (~90%) expressed either GFP or mCherry, and only a small fraction of transplanted cells fused together to make hybrid (GFP+ and mCherry+) muscle cells.

### Screening for compounds that improve myogenic progenitor cell engraftment efficiency

Bioactive lipids represent a potent class of cell-regulatory molecules that are as yet relatively understudied in stem cell and regenerative biology. Bioactive lipids signal rapidly to modulate target cell functions and can alter cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation in various adult tissues. In addition, emerging data have implicated individual lipid mediators and lipolytic enzymes in regulating hematopoietic stem cell engraftment and skeletal muscle recovery after injury.28,29,42,43 For these reasons, we chose to focus on this specific class of biomolecules in our efforts to identify compounds that enhance ZeMPC engraftment efficiency in vivo.

Myogenic progenitor cells were treated for 4 h with one of the 187 unique lipid compounds contained in the ICCB Known Bioactives Library (Table S2). Compound-treated cells were then washed, harvested, and transplanted intramuscularly into both flanks of five different casper recipient fish, with transplants performed at each of three transplanted cell doses (25, 75, or 150 cells). In these studies, recipient fish received split-dose irradiation of 15 Gy at 2 days and 1 day prior to transplantation to suppress any immune responses to the transplanted cells. Engraftment efficiency was measured by imaging casper recipients at 7 dpt (Figure 2A). Any compounds that increased engraftment efficiency (ELDA-calculated cell potency) by at least 2 times that of the simultaneously assessed control group (which received the same concentration of DMSO as the compounds’ vehicle—0.1% or 1%) were further evaluated using an irradiation-free transplantation model,41 which, due to the timing of its generation, was available only for the secondary screening approach. For secondary screening, we transplanted compound-treated cells into prkdcD3612fs casper fish, which are deficient in mature T and B cells, and assayed engraftment efficiency in the recipient fish 7 dpt. We rank-ordered the compounds according to ELDA-calculated cell potency and picked the top two, lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and niflumic acid (NFA), which showed the greatest effect in increasing ZeMPC engraftment efficiency in both assay systems (Figures 2B and 2C; Table S3), for further investigation. Notably, both LPA and NFA also increased ZeMPC engraftment efficiency in competitive transplantation assays when compared with DMSO-treated control cells (Figure S3).

### Dose titration of NFA and LPA for enhancing myogenic progenitor cell engraftment efficiency

To further assess the effects of LPA and NFA on ZeMPC engraftment, we treated cells with each compound for different durations and at different concentrations (Figure 2). Figures 2B–2G compare the engraftment efficiencies and cell potencies under these different conditions; Figures 2B and 2C show the cell potencies and compare engraftment efficiencies of different durations for different treatments. Longer DMSO treatment time resulted in lower engraftment efficiency, with 1 out of 104, 141, and 186 transplanted cells engrafted after 1, 2, and 4 h of DMSO treatment, respectively. These data suggest that under control conditions, ZeMPCs lose engraftment potential during prolonged in vitro incubation. In contrast, LPA-treated ZeMPCs showed progressively increased engraftment efficiency, over time and at each experimental time point, when compared with controls. Treatment of ZeMPCs for 1, 2, or 4 h with LPA increased the engraftment efficiency to 1.11, 1.73, and 2.3 times that of DMSO-treated cells, respectively (Figures 2B and 2C; Table S3). Similarly, while 1-h NFA treatment did not alter ZeMPC engraftment, engraftment efficiencies were increased to 2.85 and 2.64 times higher than DMSO-treated cells after 2 or 4 h of treatment, respectively (Figures 2B and 2C; Table S3). We also tested engraftment efficiencies of cells treated with DMSO (as vehicle control) or with different concentrations of LPA or NFA (Figures 2D–2G). Treatment of ZeMPCs with 5 μM LPA or 10 μM NFA yielded significantly higher (p < 0.05) engraftment efficiencies relative to vehicle-treated controls (Figures 2D–2G; Tables S4 and S5). Treatment with 0.1 μM LPA or 0.3 μM NFA did not alter the engraftment efficiency of the treated cells (Figures 2D–2G; Tables S4 and S5). Furthermore, we found that longer time and higher-concentration treatment did not result in better engraftment efficiency in comparison with 4 h of treatment with optimal concentrations of LPA or NFA (data not shown). Together, these data confirm the positive effects of both LPA and NFA on engraftment by ZeMPCs and indicate the optimal treatment time (2–4 h) to drive robust in vivo myogenic contributions from transplanted cells treated with these compounds.

### NFA and LPA have additive effects on engraftment efficiency

To determine whether a combination of NFA and LPA might show additive or synergistic effects on ZeMPC engraftment efficiency, we combined different concentrations of NFA and LPA for pre-transplantation treatment. Using the limiting dilution assay described above, we found that treatment with 0.1 μM LPA, a concentration equivalent to serum LPA levels in humans,44 did not change ZeMPC engraftment efficiency. Engraftment of myogenic progenitors treated with 0.3 μM NFA similarly showed no difference in engraftment rate compared with that of vehicle-treated controls. However, cells treated with either 0.3 μM LPA in combination with 1 μM or 10 μM NFA, or with 0.3 μM NFA in combination with 0.3 μM, 1 μM, or 10 μM LPA, showed higher engraftment efficiencies relative to experimental controls (Figures 3A–3G; Tables S3–S5). Indeed, exposure to 0.3 μM NFA combined with 0.3 μM LPA significantly increased engraftment efficiency compared with vehicle alone, while treatment with the same concentrations of these compounds individually had minimal effects (see Figures 2D–2G; Tables S4 and S5). These data suggest that NFA and LPA have additive effects on myogenic progenitor activity, since the combination of NFA and LPA at concentrations that are ineffective individually increases ZeMPC engraftment efficiency.

### NFA and LPA treatment increases mouse satellite cell engraftment efficiency

To test whether the effects of NFA and LPA on myogenic progenitor cell engraftment potential might be conserved in at least two vertebrate species, we next assessed the effects of these compounds on mouse satellite cells transplanted into pre-injured recipient tibialis anterior (TA) muscles. Satellite cells were isolated as CD45−Sca1−Mac1−CXCR4+β1-integrin+ myofiber-associated cells6,20,27,34,45–47 from FVB-Tg(CAG-eGFP) transgenic mice using our published protocol6,27,34 (Figure 4A). Sorted mouse satellite cells were exposed to NFA, LPA, or vehicle (DMSO) prior to transplant under the optimal dose conditions established using the fish model (see above; 4-h treatment at 37°C with 10 μM NFA or 5 μM LPA). Compound-treated cells were then recovered and, after washing out the media containing the compounds (NFA, LPA, or DMSO), counted and transplanted at 5,000 cells per recipient into the pre-injured TA muscles of non-transgenic FVB hosts. Four weeks after transplantation, recipients were euthanized to harvest the injected TA muscles. Muscle tissues were fixed, sectioned, stained with DAPI and wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), and imaged to quantify the number of GFP+ myofibers.20 Similar to the fish experiments, both NFA and LPA enhanced the engraftment efficiency of mouse satellite cells in these in vivo transplantation assays (Figures 4B–4D).

To further assess the engraftment potential of treated satellite cells in a relevant muscle disease model, we next transplanted 2,000 compound-treated GFP-positive satellite cells from CAG-EGFP transgenic mice48 into the pre-injured muscles of PrkdcscidDmdmdx mice.49,50 Recipient TA muscles were harvested 4 weeks after transplantation, and counting of GFP-positive myofibers demonstrated increased efficiencies of donor cell engraftment, marked by both GFP and dystrophin expression, in recipients of both LPA- and NFA-treated cells (Figures 4E and 4F). The enhanced engraftment efficiency observed in fish and mice (both wild-type [WT] and mdx recipients) indicates conserved effects of these pro-myogenic compounds on muscle precursor cells in these two vertebrate species.

To test whether transplanted muscle stem cells contribute to the endogenous pool of muscle stem cells, in addition to generating differentiated myofibers we isolated satellite cells from Tg(Pax7:ZsGreen) animals, treated these cells with vehicle (0.01% DMSO), LPA (5 μM), or NFA (10 μM), and transplanted them at 5,000 cells/muscle into pre-injured TAs of WT (C57BL/6J) mice. TA muscles were harvested 4 weeks post transplantation, and satellite cells were isolated and analyzed by flow cytometry. ZsGreen-marked cells treated with either NFA or LPA clearly contributed to the endogenous satellite cell pool at a rate that was indistinguishable from the rate of contri bution from control (DMSO-treated) cells (Figure 4G).

### NFA and LPA regulate expression of muscle development and calcium-ion-dependent genes

To gain insight into the mechanisms through which LPA and NFA treatment might enhance donor cell engraftment in vertebrate muscle, we next performed RNA-sequencing analysis in treated ZeMPCs and mouse satellite cells. Sorted zebrafish myogenic progenitors and mouse satellite cells were exposed to NFA, LPA, or vehicle (DMSO) under the optimal dose conditions (4-h treatment at 28.5°C for zebrafish myogenic progenitors and 37°C for mouse satellite cells with 10 μM NFA, 5 μM LPA, or 0.1% DMSO). Compound-treated cells were then recovered and, after washing out the media containing the compounds (NFA, LPA, or DMSO), total RNA was isolated for sequencing. Differential gene expression analysis comparing NFA-treated or LPA-treated cells with vehicle-treated cells indicated upregulation of calcium-dependent genes in response to both of these compounds in both ZeMPCs (Figure S4A) and mouse satellite cells (Figures 5A and 5B). Interestingly, treatment of mouse satellite cells with LPA upregulated myoblast fusion-related genes, including Myomaker (Tmem8c) and Ccl8. We performed qPCR for candidate genes in ZeMPCs at different time points after compound exposure to test the duration of the treatment effect. Parvalbumin 4 (pvalb4), a calcium-dependent gene upregulated in ZeMPCs treated with LPA or NFA (Figure S4A) showed peak induction at 12 h post treatment (hpt) with both 10 μM NFA and5 μM LPA (Figure S4B), and the muscle development genes myod and tnnt-2 showed peak suppression at this time point. Myh7 also showed its lowest expression at 12 hpt with 10 μM NFA, but the nadir of its expression was shifted to 24 hpt with exposure to 5 μM LPA (Figure S4B). These data suggest that both NFA and LPA exert a rapid and transient effect on the expression of both calcium-dependent and myogenesis-associated gene expression programs in compound-treated muscle progenitors.

To further evaluate the possibility suggested by these transcriptional studies that NFA and LPA may act on myogenic progenitors by increasing cytosolic calcium-ion concentration, we directly assessed intracellular calcium-ion concentration changes in ZeMPCs in the mouse myogenic cell line C2C12 and in primary mouse satellite cells in response to added compounds. ZeMPCs and C2C12 cells were incubated with Fura-2 AM, a fluorescent calcium-ion indicator, for 45 min at 28.5°C and 37°C, respectively, followed by imaging. Twenty seconds after imaging initiation, NFA or LPA was added to the cells and imaging was continued for a total of 2–3 min. Time-lapse calcium-ion imaging in ZeMPCs (Figure S5A) and mouse myogenic cell line C2C12 (Figure S5B) showed that NFA and LPA both increase the intracellular concentration of calcium ions.

To evaluate the change of intracellular calcium-ion concentration across different compound concentrations, we isolated mouse satellite cells for calcium imaging analysis. First, to establish optimal conditions, cells were sorted by FACS into 384-well plates at 10,000, 5,000, 1,500, or 500 cells per well, with eight replicates for each cell density. Subsequent incubation with Fluo4 AM, another fluorescent calcium-ion indicator, for 45 min at 37°C showed maximal signal intensity at a density of 1,500 cells per well (Figure S6). Based on these results, we next assessed intracellular calcium-ion concentration changes in primary mouse satellite cells plated at 1,500/well and exposed to varying doses of NFA and LPA. Cells were again incubated with Fluo4 AM for 45 min at 37°C followed by imaging. Different concentrations of LPA, NFA, or both compounds combined, along with DMSO (vehicle control) and ionomycin (direct calcium ionophore), were added 60 s after the beginning of imaging to quantify both baseline calcium-ion concentrations and calcium flux in response to the different treatment conditions. We calculated calcium concentrations as the area under the curve (AUC) of signal intensity and compared these values across different concentrations of each compound (Figures S7A–S7C). Calcium-ion concentrations were increased significantly relative to vehicle-treated controls in response to 1–5 μM LPA and in response to 1–10 μM NFA (Figure S7C), which, notably, overlaps with the concentrations determined to provide optimal muscle cell engraftment in zebrafish and mice (5 μM LPA and 10 μM NFA; Figures 2 and S7D). The AUC of 0.25 μM NFA combined with 0.25 μM LPA showed a boost in intracellular calcium-ion concentration in comparison with the response when each of these drugs was given individually at the same concentrations, correlating with the previously documented additive effect of NFA and LPA on engraftment (Figure 3). Interestingly, ionomycin, a positive control for calcium-ion influx in mouse satellite cells, also increased the engraftment efficiency of treated ZeMPCs (Figure S7D), consistent with a direct, mechanistic role for increased calcium signaling in enhancing the myogenic activity of transplanted muscle progenitors. We also evaluated the effects of NFA, LPA, and ionomycin on myogenic progenitor cell proliferation (5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine incorporation) and survival (TUNEL assay and 7-aminoactinomycin D staining) and found that neither LPA nor NFA altered proliferation or apoptotic rates of ex vivo exposed myogenic progenitors (Figure S8). Together, these data suggest a mechanistic model in which NFA and LPA act via similar signaling pathways that converge mechanistically to enhance myogenic engraftment through a unique calcium-ion-associated pathway.

### Transplantation of NFA-treated or LPA-treated ZeMPCs improves swimming performance in dystrophic sapje-like zebrafish

Finally, to assess the functionality of myogenic precursors exposed to NFA and/or LPA prior to muscle engraftment, we evaluated the swimming performance of sapje-like fish before and after transplantation. The sapje-like (sapc/100) fish is a dystrophin mutant and an excellent genetic and phenotypic model of human Duchenne muscular dystrophy, demonstrating histological and physiological symptoms of profound muscle degeneration.33 Recipient sapje-like fish were irradiated and injected with healthy ZeMPCs exposed prior to transplant to NFA, LPA, or vehicle alone. Cells were injected on both flanks at three dorsal points on each side—in the tail, beneath the dorsal fin, and in the trunk—with 25 cells per injection. Immediately prior to transplant, and again 7 days after transplantation, we tested muscle function in a modified Blazka-type swim chamber, in which a flow rate of approximately 5.5 L/min was introduced to test swimming performance (Figure 6). Recipient fish that were transplanted with NFA-treated or LPA-treated cells, which reproducibly show higher efficiency of myogenic engraftment (Figure 2), performed significantly better in this test when compared with fish engrafted with vehicle-treated cells (Figures 6B–6E). Because we transplanted only the treated cells after removal of all compounds, we conclude from these studies that the swimming performance of these transplanted sapje-like fish was improved as a result of better engraftment by NFA-treated or LPA-treated ZeMPCs.

## DISCUSSION

Using the uniquely quantitative, rapid, and integrated cross-species screening system described here, we have identified regulators of vertebrate muscle cell engraftment and established a platform for discovery of pro-myogenic molecules that act directly on muscle precursor cells and target a stem cell-specific cellular function (in vivo engraftment). Multiple studies, including this one, demonstrate the vastly superior capacity of the most primitive subset of muscle precursor cells to contribute productively to muscle repair in transplantation and regeneration assays, particularly in comparison with their differentiated daughters, despite the fact that the two types of cells often show equivalent proliferative capacity in ex vivo culture.9,18,20,47,51 Strategies that rely entirely on ex vivo screening for numeric increases in cell number52,53 after long-term (i.e., days, as opposed to only hours in our study) exposure to added chemicals could miss potent stem cell-specific compounds whose effects are obscured by the presence of non-stem cells in these cultures. The outcomes of such screens also are highly influenced by the precise culture conditions used,54 and might instead favor the identification of compounds that increase cell numbers overall but do not specifically expand or preserve the unique engraftment functions of the muscle stem cell compartment. On the other hand, the use of classical myogenic engraftment assays as a primary outcome measure in chemical screening approaches has been eschewed by most investigators in the research community, due in large part to the prohibitive costs in terms of the time and resources it would require. Most studies to date that have identified single molecules capable of increasing the ex vivo yield of satellite cells or enhancing muscle regenerative potential have instead utilized expanded cells and candidate-based approaches, informed in some cases by genetic or transcriptional screening.16,21,55–58

In this study, we sought to overcome this barrier to direct screening on stem cell-specific functions in muscle by developing a cross-species approach, first evaluating the myogenic effects of library compounds in a zebrafish transplantation system and then further assessing “hits” in more standard mouse models. We decided to focus on bioactive lipids in this study because, while they were well represented in our chemical library, they have not been well studied for their effects on stem cell function. Thus, by focusing on bioactive lipids, we could provide a comprehensive assessment of a specific (and understudied) class of biomolecules that would likely reveal novel biology. In addition, we were aware that bioactive lipids can signal very rapidly, which we thought would be an advantageous feature for our screening strategy, whereby precursor cells are exposed to test compounds for only 4 h before washing and transplantation. Finally, we were compelled by emerging data implicating individual lipid mediators (such as prostaglandin E2 and epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and lipolytic enzymes in modulating hematopoietic stem cell engraftment and skeletal muscle recovery after injury, respectively.28–31

A significant advantage of our cross-species approach is the increased throughput afforded by use of the zebrafish system (a total of approximately 14,000 recipient fish were used in this study) and the greater time efficiency of zebrafish myogenesis, which enables specification of myogenic progenitors within 2–3 days and readout of in vivo engraftment within a week. In contrast, analogous mouse and human systems require more than 1 month for each step.34 Furthermore, extensive data demonstrating the evolutionary conservation of vertebrate myogenesis and our prior work documenting the strong predictive power of the zebrafish system to identify bioactive molecules that similarly regulate mammalian myogenesis34 provided a strong rationale for this cross-species approach. We further increased the specificity and rigor of this platform by incorporating highly sensitive limiting dilution assays for quantitative assessment of engrafting cell frequencies within populations of compound-exposed cells. We undertook an unbiased assessment of all lipid mediators contained within a focused library of bioactive compounds and, by restricting compound exposure to ex vivo pre-transplantation treatment of myogenic progenitor cells, removing compounds by washing prior to transplant, we were able to eliminate any potential toxicity or indirect (bystander) effect of the compounds on the host environment. These features resulted in a robust assay system for studying muscle engraftment.

Using this in vivo cross-system strategy, we screened 187 compounds in zebrafish and selected the top two—NFA, a Food and Drug Administration-approved non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), and LPA, a bioactive phospholipid—for further testing in mice. We documented improved engraftment after pre-transplantation treatment with each of these lipid mediators in both zebrafish and mice, and further identified overlapping cell physiological effects and transcriptional consequences of these two compounds. These observations reinforce the notion that our approach optimally leverages evolutionary similarities between vertebrates to enable more efficient drug identification.

LPA is a prominent member of the lysophospholipid family, an endogenous class of lipid mediators known to act through sets of specific G-protein-coupled receptors named LPAR1–LPAR6.59 LPA may pass through the cell membrane60 and may also be generated from membrane phospholipids.61 Prior studies have implicated LPA in regulating intracellular calcium-ion concentrations, consistent with the results presented here, as well as in the control of cell migration, adhesion, survival, development, and proliferation.62–65 In studies of cancer cells, LPA’s effects on cell migration have been attributed to its stimulation of Rho activation and actin depolymerization via increases in intracellular calcium-ion concentration.63,66 In muscle cells, LPA also has been shown to stimulate the migration and proliferation of cultured myoblasts,42 with its effects mediated in part through sphingosine kinase and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors; however, the impact of LPA on the regenerative activities of muscle satellite cells in vivo have not previously been assessed. The studies presented here reveal that LPA exposure significantly enhances the engraftment capacities of muscle progenitor cells from both zebrafish and mice, concomitant with increases in cytoplasmic calcium concentration and alterations of myogenic gene expression.

Like LPA, NFA exposure also enhanced the engraftment activities of muscle progenitors across species and induced similar calcium flux and transcriptional alterations. Unlike LPA, which is produced endogenously in fish and mice, NFA is a synthetic compound whose cellular receptor remains unknown. NFA is a member of the NSAID family and can inhibit both phospholipase A2 67 and cyclooxygenases such as COX-2.68,69 NFA is frequently used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis to reduce pain and suppress inflammation; however, its potential utility for augmenting the contributions of transplanted myogenic progenitors to regenerating muscle has not previously been assessed. Interestingly, prior studies testing the in vivo effects of NSAID administration on endogenous muscle repair have reported both pro-regenerative29 and anti-regenerative30 impacts. This suggests differences in the specific actions of individual NSAIDs and/or pleiotropy of their action on different cell types in vivo. In this regard, the ex vivo exposure and transplantation strategy implemented here presents a distinct advantage, avoiding such complications by restricting compound exposure to only myogenic precursor cells and thereby revealing the particular effects of these molecules on stem cell-specific regenerative activities.

In our studies, we found that both NFA and LPA trigger rapid increases in intracellular calcium-ion concentration within treated muscle progenitors, consistent with prior observations in other cell types.65,70 Notably, these effects of LPA and NFA were additive, potentially reflecting previously reported differences in the mechanisms by which they impact calcium flux. In particular, while NFA triggers increases in intracellular calcium by inducing the release of calcium ions from intracellular stores, increases of intracellular calcium seen with LPA treatment have been attributed to influx of calcium ions from extracellular sources.71,72 We posit that exposure to NFA and LPA together enables mobilization of calcium from both intracellular and extracellular depots, resulting in an additive effect.

We also found that LPA increases the expression of myoblast fusion regulators and effectors, including Ccl873 and Myomaker (also known as Mymk and Tmem8c).74,75 Such effects may promote the increased contribution of LPA-treated cells to the formation of multinucleated fibers in transplant recipients. Moreover, in addition to its effects promoting myogenic cell fusion, Ccl8 also has been implicated in promoting myogenic differentiation76 and as a positive regulator of the release of sequestered calcium ions into the cytosol.77 Thus, induction of Ccl8 by LPA may further enhance the calcium-mobilizing and pro-myogenic activities of this compound.

As an ultimate test of the ability of compounds discovered in our screening system to stimulate productive contributions to regenerative myogenesis by transplanted muscle precursor cells, we examined the impact on dystrophic mdx mice and sapje-like fish of engraftment with NFA-treated or LPA-treated cells, simulating a clinical cell therapy scenario. Engraftment with either NFA-treated or LPA-treated muscle progenitors resulted in significant engraftment of dystrophin-positive muscle fibers in recipient mice, and improvements in swimming performance of the recipient fish in comparison with control fish receiving equivalent doses (25 cells per injection at each of six different injection sites) of vehicle-treated ZeMPCs. Given our consistent observation that LPA and NFA treatment increases the engraftment efficiency of donor ZeMPCs, together with the fact that compound exposure was restricted to the pre-transplantation period, with careful washing to remove any residual compound prior to cell injection, we conclude from these studies that the improvement in swimming performance reflects an improved engraftment efficiency, with no direct effect on the recipient muscle tissue. Such ex vivo chemical treatment approaches could be applied in clinical cell therapy as a strategy to boost the per-cell regenerative output of ex vivo expanded or pluripotent-cell-derived human muscle progenitors.

This study provides three lines of evidence suggesting similar and synergistic signaling mechanisms of NFA and LPA: First, we show that both compounds elicit a rapid and robust increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figures S4–S7) and that calcium ionophore, which acts directly to stimulate calcium influx, similarly enhances muscle engraftment properties of ex vivo exposed muscle progenitors (Figure S7) without impacting their proliferative activity or survival (Figure S8). Second, we performed RNA-sequencing analysis of myogenic progenitors treated with each compound and identified a suite of similarly regulated genes (Figures 5 and S4), including known myogenic regulatory factors, as well as some differentially regulated pathways. Finally, we performed co-treatment studies and showed that co-administration of subthreshold doses of NFA + LPA elicited a similar functional response to optimized (higher) doses of each compound individually (Figure 3). These studies indicate that NFA and LPA act via similar, though not identical, signaling pathways and that they converge mechanistically to induce transient increases in intracellular Ca2+, which in turn enhances myogenic engraftment of muscle progenitors.

In summary, this work establishes a screening platform for the discovery of pro-myogenic compounds that act specifically on muscle stem cells and target a muscle stem cell-specific function: myogenic engraftment after in vivo transplantation. Applying this platform to interrogate the effects of lipid mediators, a relatively understudied class of biomolecules, we discovered two—NFA and LPA—that enhance the in vivo engraftment efficiency of both in vitro expanded embryo-derived zebrafish muscle cells and freshly isolated mouse muscle satellite cells. We further showed that LPA and NFA also significantly increase intracellular calcium-ion concentration in zebrafish muscle cells, C2C12 mouse muscle cells, and mouse satellite cells and that the combination of these two lipids at low concentrations had an additive effect and enhanced muscle progenitor cell engraftment efficiency. Finally, we evaluated the functionality of transplanted cells and showed that transplantation of NFA- and LPA-treated muscle progenitors rescued dystrophin expression in mdx mice and improved muscle function, measured by swimming performance, in dystrophic sapje-like zebrafish. This study indicates that pre-transplantation drug treatment can be used to improve muscle cell therapy approaches and rescue muscle function through progenitor cell engraftment in muscular dystrophies.

### Limitations of the study

Our studies suggest that NFA and LPA act via similar Ca2+-associated signaling pathways to enhance the engraftment of transplanted muscle progenitor cells. However, future work will be needed to clarify their direct molecular targets and explain mechanistically how transient exposure to these compounds translates into a sustained alteration in engraftment function that persists even after removal of the chemical and termination of Ca2+ induction. Additionally, as our primary screening assay relied on embryonic ZeMPCs generated by in vitro culture of blastomeres, compounds that act solely on adult muscle progenitors or only on mammalian cells would not have been selected in our screen. Finally, although our system provides a significant advantage over wholly ex vivo muscle cell systems in terms of time, cost, and interrogation of in vivo muscle engraftment, it still requires direct hands-on effort imposing a limitation on the number of compounds that can be screened. Future innovations to automate ZeMPC production, culture, transplant, and live-imaging-based screening of myogenic engraftment would significantly accelerate the throughput of this assay system and enable screening of much larger compound libraries and additional chemical diversity.

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND SUBJECT DETAILS

#### Fish housing, husbandry and fish transgenic lines

All fish used in these experiments were housed in 3.5L tanks with recirculating water and kept at 10 fish per liter. Water quality was kept at a constant 1250 μS, pH 7.5, and a water temperature of 28.5°C. Fish were fed Gemma Micro 500 at approximately 5% body weight per day and housed under a photoperiod of 14hr-light, 10hr-dark cycle. All fish were bred and housed following standard zebrafish husbandry.78 In this study, we used the following transgenic fish lines: Tg(myf5-GFP), Tg(mylz2-GFP), and Tg(mylz2-mCherry) for zebrafish blastomere culture and ZeMPCs generation. Tg(MHC-casper) and Tg(prkdcD3612fs) (casper-strain) as recipients in the screen experiment and Tg(sapje-like (sapc/100) for function study.

#### Mouse husbandry and handling

FVB-Tg(CAG-eGFP) mice (Stock 003516; RRID:IMSR_JAX:003516), FVB/NJ mice (Stock 001800), and Prkdcscid Dmdmdx mice (Stock 018018) were obtained from the Jackson Laboratory. (C57BL/CAG-EGFP) mice were in house.48 All mice were housed in the Animal Facility of Harvard University and all the experiments and protocols were performed in compliance with the institutional guidelines of Harvard University. These studies used adult (8–16 weeks of age) male mice.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Culture and myogenesis of dissociated zebrafish blastomere cells

Myogenic progenitor cells were generated in vitro from mylz2-GFP, mylz2-mCherry (RRID:ZFIN_ZDB-ALT-071016–1) or myf5-GFP;mylz2-mCherry embryos using our published protocols34 with minor changes. 20–30 embryos were used to dissociate the blastomere cells and grown in a zESC medium composed of 70% LDF medium (50% Leibowitz’s L-15 (Gibco), 35% DMEM (Gibco), and 15% Ham’s F-12 (Gibco)), with 20% embryo extract and 10% FBS; these were supplemented with 2 ng/ml recombinant human FGF basic protein (Sigma-Aldrich), 15 mM sodium bicarbonate, 15 mM HEPES (Gibco),1% L-glutamine (Gibco), 10 nM sodium selenite (Sigma-Aldrich), 1% N2 (Gibco), 2% B27 (Gibco), and 0.1 mg/ml Primocin (Invivogen). Cells were cultured at 28°C without CO2 for 48 hours.

#### Chemical treatments and zebrafish in vivo screen

Lipids from the ICCB Known Bioactives Library (enzolifesciences.com/BML-2840/iccb-known-bioactives-library) (see Table S2) were diluted at a 1:100 ratio in transplantation media (zESC medium without bFGF and FBS) and added to prewashed in vitro expanded muscle cells. NFA (Cayman and Santa Cruz Biotechnology) and LPA (Cayman and Santa Cruz Biotechnology) were used for secondary screening experiments. DMSO concentration was 1% for the primary screen (consistent with 1:100 ratio dilution of the library), and 0.1% for the other experiments including secondary screen, competitive transplantation, mouse experiments and functional study. Zebrafish cells were incubated with lipids for 4 hours at 28.5°C, followed by washing out the media and drugs, harvesting the cells, and splitting into 3 cell doses for transplantation. 4- to 8-month-old casper recipients received split-dose irradiation of 15 Gy each, either 2 days or 1 day before transplantation. For LDA screening, cells from each group were split into 3 doses and transplanted into each side of 5 pre-irradiated casper recipient fish or 5 non-irradiated prkdc-mutant recipient zebrafish. The prkdc-mutant zebrafish line was available only after we initiated the primary screen. Because irradiation could interfere with muscle cell engraftment,79 we used the prkdc-mutant zebrafish for repeat experiments and to confirm the validity of the primary screening system. At 7 dpt, recipients were anaesthetized using a previously described method80 and imaged using a fluorescent stereo microscope (Leica M165 FC). Successful engraftment was defined as the presence of mylz2-GFP+/mylz2-mCherry+ fibers. Variation in different experiments is caused by inherent variability in the in vitro ZeMPC derivation procedure, which results in differences in engrafting cell frequency across different derivation attempts. To mitigate the impact of such experimental variation on our screening results, we only compared LDA results for cells derived from the same cultures and included comparison to a vehicle-treated experimental control in every transplantation experiment. Chemical treated cell potency and vehicle-treated cell potency were measured and analysed using the Extreme Limiting Dilution Analysis (ELDA) software.36

#### Zebrafish tissue sampling, staining, and imaging

Adult zebrafish recipients were euthanized at 7 dpt. The dissected body trunks were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by cryoprotection with 30% sucrose solution at 4°C overnight. Tissue specimens were embedded with Leica OTC tissue-freezing medium (Leica 14020108926) and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen, then sectioned with a cryostat at −25°C (Leica CM1860). The sections were transferred to a room temperature Opaque-coated slide (VWR® Superfrost® Plus Micro Slide 48311–703), followed by air-drying overnight. Sections were demembranated, blocked, and stained with 0.5% Triton X-100, 3% BSA, and DAPI, respectively. Sections were protected by embedding in mounting medium (Vectashield H-1400) and covered with a coverslip. The mounted slides were stored at 4°C in a light-protected condition to preserve the fluorescence before imaging. Images were acquired using Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 and Zeiss 880 in the Harvard Center for Biological Imaging. The captured images were processed quantitatively with Zen, ImageJ, and MATLAB.

#### Functional assay setup and swimming performance measurement

Juvenile zebrafish from a sapje-like transgenic line were fin-clipped and genotyped to identify heterozygotes, while the swimming assay was performed at the adult stage. The homozygote sapje-like fish cannot survive until the adult stage; thus, the swimming performance was conducted in heterozygote recipients. The impaired swimming performance of the sapje-like fish was reported previously by Vieira et al., 2017.81 It has been shown that sapje-like (sapcl100) fish shows a similar phenotype in muscle tearing and lack the dystrophin protein.33 A flow-through modified Blazka-type swim chamber was created using a horizontal acrylic tank with dimensions of 350 mm l × 47mm w × 90mm d. System water, equal in quality to recirculating water in housing tanks, was introduced into one side of the swim chamber at a flow rate of approximately 5.5L min−1. Water flow funnelled through a honeycombed grid composed of 50 vinyl tubes (6.35mm 0D, 3.97mm ID × 50mm l). This created a laminar flow through the remaining 250mm length of the swim chamber × 50mm deep × 47mm wide, limiting fish to a swimming area of approximately 587.5 cubic cm = 0.6L. Another 1000-micron baffle was positioned downstream of the tunnel to prevent any fish from flowing out of the three drainage points located at the far end of the swim chamber. Adult sapje-like fish were netted out of their holding tanks and placed inside the already flowing swim chamber before and 7 days after transplantation. A high-definition Nikon D3100 digital camera was used to record individual fish’s swimming performance, filmed at 30 frames per second for a total of 3 minutes. If a fish reached a point of fatigue where it could no longer maintain its position in the swim chamber, the fish was swept downstream onto the 1000-micron baffle located at the far end of the tank. A plastic transfer pipette was used to assist the fish off the baffle if it could not free itself and continue swimming. The raw digital file was then analysed for movement within the swim area. The distance from the flow source was quantified using MATLAB (MathWorks; RRID:SCR_001622).

#### Mouse satellite cell isolation, treatment, and transplantation

Mouse satellite cells were isolated as previously described.6,27,34 25 μl (0.03 mg/ml) of cardiotoxin (CDTX) (Latoxan) was injected 24h prior to transplantation into the TA muscle of recipient mice (FVB/NJ or Prkdcscid Dmdmdx), to stimulate a regenerative response.20 GFP tagged satellite cells were isolated and plated on a collagen/laminin-coated plate and treated with NFA (10 μM), LPA (5 μM) or DMSO, as the vehicle control, in culture media for 4 hours at 37°C. The culture media contained 78% F10 (GIBCO), 20% horse serum (Atlanta Biologics), 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco), and 5 ng/ml bFGF (Sigma). After 4 hours, cells were washed with DPBS, harvested, and counted, followed by transplantation of 5000 and 2000 satellite cells intramuscularly into the CDTX pre-injured TA of FVB/NJ or Prkdcscid Dmdmdx recipients, respectively.

#### Mouse TA sampling, cryosectioning, staining, and imaging

Transplanted TAs were dissected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by cryoprotection with a 30% sucrose solution. Next, the TAs were washed with DPBS and frozen in pre-incubated isopentane in liquid nitrogen for 30 seconds followed by a 30-second incubation in liquid nitrogen. Frozen TA muscles were sectioned using a cryostat at −25°C (Leica CM1850) at 10 μm thickness. Sections were stained with dystrophin (Sigma, D8043), WGA (Thermo Fisher) and DAPI (Thermo Fisher) and embedded in mounting medium (Vectashield, vector laboratories). Images were acquired using Axio Scan.Z1 (Zeiss) and Zeiss 880 in the Harvard Center for Biological Imaging. Captured images were processed quantitatively with ZEN and ImageJ.

#### Culture of the mouse myogenic cell line C2C12

Cells were grown at 37°C in growth media: DMEM (Gibco), %10 FBS and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco).

#### Calcium imaging in ZeMPCs and C2C12 cells

ZeMPCs or C2C12 cells were incubated with Fura-2, AM (Thermo Fisher Sci F1225), a cell permeant fluorescent calcium ion indicator, for 45 minutes at 28.5°C, followed by imaging with Celldiscoverer7 Microscope (Zeiss). ZeMPCs were incubated in transplantation media (zESC medium without bFGF and FBS to simulate the transplantation experiment) and C2C12 cells at 37°C in growth media. 20 seconds after imaging initiation the indicated compound(s) or vehicle was added to the cells and imaging was continued for a total of 2–3 minutes.

#### Calcium imaging in mouse satellite cells

Satellite cells were isolated from wild-type mice (FVB/NJ) and sorted into 384 well plates in culture media. Cells were incubated overnight at 37°C. The next day, cells were incubated with Fluo-4 AM (Thermo Fisher Sci F14201), a fluorescent calcium ion indicator, for 45 minutes at 37°C, followed by imaging of the entire plate with the FDSS 7000ex functional drug screening system (Hamamatsu) in the BCH assay development and screening facility.

#### RNA sequencing

Isolated mouse muscle satellite cells and ZeMPCs were used to prepare RNA after in vitro chemical treatment. Total RNA was isolated from 2000 cells per replicate and 3 replicates per treatment by the micro RNeasy kit (QIAGEN) for both mouse muscle satellite cells and ZeMPCs. cDNA was prepared using SMART Seq v4 Ultra Low RNA-Seq kit for 48 reactions (Takara) and a Nextera kit was used for library construction. FASTQ files for samples were processed in tophat-cufflinks workflow in a Linux server operating system to output gene-level abundance estimates and statistical inference as gene-level raw counts. Those raw counts for samples were input into the cuffdiff for differential gene expression analysis. The assigned GEO accession number for the RNA sequencing data is GSE143801.

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

All results are presented as raw data or mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) where indicated. Statistical analysis was performed using the LDA test to measure the number of engrafting cells (potent cells), two-way ANOVA to test the murine engraftment efficiency in different groups and paired t tests to test the swimming performance in the function study (Graphpad Prism®; version 8.3). Sample size, replicate number, treatment concentration and/or treatment duration for each experiment are indicated in the figure legends. Results with p values of less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant: * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; ns., not significant.

#### Gene expression analysis

Up to 2.5 μg total RNA, extracted from ZeMPCs using RNeasy micro kits (QIAGEN), was used to synthesis the cDNA using SuperScript™ VILO™ cDNA Synthesis Kit (Thermo Fishher). The gene expression was measured using Fast SYBR® Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) and the fluorescence was detected by QuantStudio™ 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Life technologies). All reactions were performed in triplicates and 18-S was used as a house-keeping control. Primers used in this experiment are: 18s CGCTAGTTGGCATCGTTTATG (F), CGGAGGTTCGAAGACGATCA (R), pvalb4–2 CGGGATTGATGAGTTCGCTGCC (F), GATGA AAATGGGAGGTGTTGGGA (R), myod AACATTACAGTGGAGACTCTG (F), GTCATAGCTGTCCGTCTTC (R), myh7 TGGTGCACATCAGACAAGGC (F), TCTCACCTTCACGACTGACG (R) and tnnt2d CCAAGCACCAAAAATCCCTG (F), CTGCTCGCCTCTTTTCGATT (R).

Abstract: The Capitalist Spatial Matrix: A Political Theory of the Built Environment

This dissertation develops a theory of the built environment and its role in the reproduction

and stabilization of capitalist society. It begins by demonstrating that despite consistent engagement

with that problematic, the past fifty years of critical socio-spatial scholarship has yet to produce an

adequate account of that relationship. To develop one, the dissertation then proceeds in two parts.

The first part of the dissertation is pitched at a high level of conceptual abstraction and considers the

place of the built environment in capitalist society across three conceptual axes: crisis, articulation,

and interpellation. Through dialogues with key figures in the history of political and social thought—

ranging from Johann Heinrich von Thünen and G.F.W. Hegel to David Harvey and Stuart Hall—it

demonstrates that the built environment should be understood as central to (1) the production and

resolution of crises that arise across capitalism’s normatively differentiated abodes of social and

ecological work; (2) the articulation of capitalist society’s necessary and contingent parts, especially

the articulation of racialized and gendered forms of ascriptive hierarchization in capitalist contexts;

and (3) the interpellation of differentiated capitalist subjectivities.

Part II of the dissertation concretizes the theoretical agenda developed in Part I, turning to a

close reading of two episodes in the history of American heterodox political economic thought to do

so. First, it engages the “black belt debate” of the 1930s, which sought to make sense of the

survivals of slavery after Reconstruction and the potentiality of black self-determination in the US

south. In so doing, it attends specifically to the spatial presuppositions and implications of that

debate, and to what it reveals regarding the role of the built environment in mediating capitalist


<!-- Page 6 -->


iv

crises. Second, it engages the US iteration of the “domestic labor debate” of the 1970s and 1980s.

The dissertation argues that several participants within that debate relied heavily on spatial concepts

and categories, and that their interventions help to demonstrate the role of the built environment in

the articulation of race, gender, and capitalism’s constitutive dynamics, as well as the built

environment’s role in the interpellation of differentiated capitalist subjectivities. The dissertation

then concludes with a brief discussion of the normative implications of this account of the role of

the built environment in the reproduction of capitalist society.

## Preface

Prior to the 1970s, the archive of scholarship in political and social thought had given

relatively short shrift to the built environment. Of course, there were moments in which the built

environment appeared in that archive, sometimes rather plainly. This is particularly true of the

landmark texts that defined the middle part of the twentieth century. Hannah Arendt, in her 1960

essay “What is Freedom,” argued that freedom was not “an attribute of the will,” but “an accessory

of doing and acting” that required its own “space of appearance”—or its own built environment.1

And Martin Heidegger, to name but one additional example, famously suggested in Being and Time

(1927) that “the ‘subject’ (Dasein)” is “ontologically” spatial.2 He argued that human existence has

its “Being-in-the-world as its essential state,” and, as such, that the built environment supports it in its

average everydayness.3 But these invocations hardly constitute serious or extended engagements with

the built environment itself. And moving further back in the history of political and social thought,

the visibility of the built environment becomes only more opaque.4 A generous reader could attempt

to identify moments in which the built environment is present in its absence prior to the twentieth

century. We can read texts like Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics and consider how the built environment

shapes the processes of habituation that make virtuousness. We can read the long history of political

other than its own.”5 But in so doing, we would only further substantiate our point.6

Since the 1970s, however, the built environment has become a key object of intellectual and

In fact, a cohort of dissident scholars emerged in the 1970s and 1980s that took the built

capitalist society’s inherent and recurrent crises are produced and resolved; that the necessary and

contingent parts of capitalist society are conjoined and articulated; and through which differentiated,

The built environment is thus not simply another name for the environment in general, even

if it has long since been impossible to distinguish between environments that bear the imprint of

human sociality and those that do not.10 It is certainly the case that “nature,” if it ever did exist, no

longer does, and that the entirety of what surrounds us bears the mark of human life. And yet, the

built environment is, in my account, but a specific part of the environment at large—it is that

relatively fixed and immobile part that was produced in the service of specific forms of individual

and/or collective use. The built environment maintains a distinctive temporality: it preempts and

interpellates us.11 It includes plantations and conservation areas just as much as sidewalks and

apartment complexes, but it excludes the atmosphere, rain, and the squirrel outside of my window.

And, as I will argue in the pages to come, the built environment stands at the center of the

mediation, materialization, and concretization of that conceptual abstraction that has occupied so

much of our thought within political and social theory: capitalism. Without the built environment

capitalism is a theoretical abstraction; through it, it becomes capitalist society.

The implications of this account are more than “merely” theoretical. The theoretical

armature that I will develop throughout this dissertation sheds critical light on longstanding debates

on the history and geography of capitalist development, just as it does empirical scholarship on the

built environment within geography, urban studies, sociology, and beyond. In reimagining the role

of the built environment in the reproduction of capitalist society, this dissertation recasts empirical

work on topics ranging from housing and homelessness to segregation and the potentiality of

“sustainable urban development.” It holds crucial normative implications too. The basic insight that

## The detour of abstraction

If you consider the vast archive of scholarship on capitalism and its reproduction for long

enough, a curious feature begins to appear. It becomes clear that this literature, which is now (at

least) a century and a half old, and which spans nearly all domains of humanistic inquiry, does not

take very seriously the fact that capitalist societies invariably contain relations that make them

capitalist—by dint of the fact that they are, indeed, describable as “capitalist”—and relations that do

not. In fact, upon close reflection, scholarship within this domain tends to not simply obscure the

fact that capitalist societies always contain necessary features that define them as capitalist, and

contingent features that do not; but, going further still, it tends to fall into one of three intellectual

camps, each implicated in this broader tendency, albeit in a distinctive way. Accounts of capitalism

and its reproduction tend to be either (1) “obscurantist,” (2) “essentialist,” or (3) “reductionist.” The

first cohort of scholars—“the obscurantists”—obscure the fact that capitalist societies are always

constituted by necessary features and logically contingent dimensions. This scholarship engages the

reproduction of capitalist society in name, but when read closely it does not provide an account of

the abstract-theoretical (or necessary) features that define capitalist society, or a “theory of capital,”

at all. These scholars attend to the “complex states of causal codetermination” that comprise

capitalist societies, and to the remaking of these states over time.12 And yet, in so doing, they

obscure any clear distinction between which aspects of their “abstracted unit” are necessary to its

definition as capitalist, and which are not.13 They concern themselves with the making and remaking

of complex totalities that appear to be comprised of elements that “have no immediate or necessary

Argument, structure, method

So far, I have provided an initial critique of the broad literature on capitalist reproduction,

and an initial critique of the received literature within radical geography and critical socio-spatial

theory. I now turn to an overview of how I will answer the central question of this dissertation: that

is, how I will theorize the role of the built environment in the mediation, materialization, and

reproduction of capitalist society. This dissertation is structured in two parts, one primarily

theoretical and one primarily intellectual-historical, with the latter aiming to concretize and clarify

the theoretical arguments developed in Part I. The first part of the dissertation is comprised of three

chapters, with each speaking to a distinctive role that the built environment plays in the

reproduction of capitalist society, as it is conceived here. Chapter two, titled “Crisis,” sets out to

provide an account of the necessary dimensions that define all capitalist contexts, and of the role of

the built environment in their reproduction. To do so, I will take up a critical reading of David

Harvey’s landmark account, briefly sketched above, which I take to be the most influential effort to

reproducing the constituent features of capitalist society, but what his account holds from view.

## Crisis

Capitalism, as a social and ecological system, does not simply produce a world in its own

image. It produces, in the words of British Marxist and state theorist John Holloway, a “law-bound

world.” Of course, there is no reason why such a law-bound world should exist. As Holloway notes,

“[t]here is no inherent reason why the production of wealth should follow any set of laws.” Our

shared social life and the process of producing goods to facilitate our material reproduction can

proceed in any number of ways, so long as it meets the corporeal demands of bodily reproduction—

an argument that Holloway himself also makes. And yet, in the capitalist world, things are decidedly

different. In this world, we do not simply produce “wealth,” but “wealth” in the form of commodities.

Because these commodities are “produced for exchange,” this process “imposes the need to

produce them with labour that is socially necessary, [creating] a whole world of functional

The hidden abodes of capitalist space

This chapter has developed a relatively straightforward argument. I have suggested that

Harvey inaugurated a theoretical revolution beginning in the 1970s in and through his theorization

of the role of the built environment in the reproduction of capital and its constituent dynamics. In

his understanding of capitalism’s spatial fix, Harvey was able to break crisis theory out of the “a-

spatial mould” in which it is often cast, and to move beyond even those spatializations provided by

figures like Hegel, von Thünen, Luxemburg, and Lenin.219 My contention is thus surely not that

Harvey’s theorization should be dismissed out of hand. That said, in the remainder of this chapter, I

will develop a critique of it. I will move beyond Harvey’s emphasis on the relationship between the

built environment and the hidden abode of production—which is Harvey’s primary concern, insofar

as he attends narrowly to crises of overaccumulation that have their roots in the realm of commodity

production—and turn our focus to its relation to the hidden abodes behind the abode of production

as well. I will insist that to make sense of the role of the built environment in the reproduction of

capital at the highest level of conceptual abstraction, we must make sense of its place within

capitalism as an institutionalized social order that is necessarily constituted by both foreground and

background abodes. We must revisit our understanding of the necessary dimensions and dynamics

that constitute capitalism at a high level of abstraction, and the built environment’s relation to them.

But, with that said, we must now ask: what exactly does it mean to posit capitalism as an

institutionalized social order, constituted by multiple hidden abodes?

To answer this question, we would do well to turn to the political philosopher and critical

theorist Nancy Fraser. Fraser has worked tirelessly over the last decade to establish the claim that

capitalism is not—as it might appear in Harvey’s account—merely an economic system; but rather,

Conclusion

This chapter has set out to articulate several closely linked arguments. It began by taking

stock of David Harvey’s conceptualization of the role of the built environment in the reproduction

of capital’s constituent dynamics. It situated Harvey—as he himself has done—in a long history of

efforts to spatialize crisis theory, which spans the work of Hegel and von Thünen, and Luxemburg

and Lenin. It emphasized the genuine theoretical revolution that he inaugurated relative to those

sources with his conceptualization of the built environment. With his account in view, the re-

spatialization of capital emerged as endemic (well beyond the historical moment of imperialism and

settler colonialism), and as hardly limited to the forms of external re-territorialization that are

propelled by the “external coercive” determinations of capital.288 This chapter then developed an

account of the role of the built environment in the reproduction of capital’s necessary or constituent

parts that takes seriously those normatively differentiated background spheres that constitute

capitalism as an institutionalized social order, and that fall from view in Harvey’s account. I argued

that the capitalist spatial matrix emerges through—or appears at the same time as—the ongoing and

uneven re-articulation of capitalism’s foreground and background abodes. Integrating the language

of underproduction into our lexicon, I suggested that capitalist crises are driven either by

overproduction in the foreground of exploitation and/or by the underproduction of non-

commodified and/or under-capitalized inputs produced via capitalism’s background abodes. And,

ultimately, I argued that both of these crisis tendencies are spatially constituted and resolved,

## Articulation

It is unlikely that capitalist society requires “race” or “gender” for its expanded reproduction.

Even if capital’s requisite background conditions of possibility, sketched in the preceding chapter,

have long been tightly linked to the oppression of racialized and gendered subjects—such that those

forms of distinction within capitalist society invariably carry the weight of that historical

association—it hardly seems conceivable that capital necessitates specific forms of ascriptive difference

in any respect. Following Julian Go’s brief but highly influential intervention on the tensions at the

core of the “racial capitalism” debate, we might say that insofar as scholars have arrived at that

position—at the claim that capital requires race and gender as distinctive forms of ascriptive

differentiation—they have done so in a way that is troublingly inattentive to the distinction between

a theory of capital and a theory of capitalism. As Go puts it, a theory of capital is principally concerned with

the development of “a formalized and abstract representation of the inner workings of capital…its

contradictions, and its necessary demise through a series of central categories that capture the key

elements of the capitalist system.” And, by contrast, a theory of capitalism aims at precisely the

opposite. It intends to speak directly to “capitalist development and dynamics in their empirical

specificity. It is meant to explain and describe specific capitalist formations and developments as

they really exist in the world, not their abstract conceptual form.”306 And with this distinction in

view, the suggestion that capitalism necessarily carries with it processes of racialization and gendered

hierarchization—that they are necessary to a theory of capital—appears to simply reproduce a kind of

“ex post facto functionalism” in which the centrality of those forms of difference in capitalist history

is read as proof of their place in the “inner workings of capital” itself.307

306 Julian Go, “Three Tensions in the Theory of Racial Capitalism,” Sociological Theory 39, no. 1 (2021): 42.

Revisiting “articulation”: from Althusser to Stuart Hall

The conceptual history of “articulation” can be told in several ways. In the opening pages of

his recent overview, Power of Articulation (2023), Matti Kortesoja indicates as much indirectly.

Therein, he moves swiftly from the concept’s invocation in anatomy, to phonetics, to Saussure’s

notion of “articulated speech” (“gegliederte Sprache”), and well beyond, tracking its use across a range

of disciplinary contexts and historical-geographical conjunctures.314 In considering the articulation of

capital and ascriptive difference, however, the most relevant place to start is surely with the work of

Louis Althusser. After all, it was Althusser that first latched onto Marx’s use of “Gliederung” (rooted

in the German for limb, “Glied”); rendered it as “articulated whole” or “articulated combination”;

and situated the concept at the center of his reading and explication of Marxist philosophy and

critique of Hegelian dialectics. It is this usage that has come to structure the articulationist literature

on the problem of ascriptive difference—not least Stuart Hall’s enduring and highly influential

account. If we want to make sense of—and go beyond—Hall’s landmark theorization of the

articulation of capital and logically contingent processes of ascriptive hierarchization, we would thus

do well to begin by turning our attention to the development of the concept of articulation in the

work of Althusser. We would do well to begin, more specifically, with Althusser’s earliest uses of the

term—and with texts like “On the Materialist Dialectic” (first published in 1963), “Marxism and

Humanism” (first published in 1964), and Reading Capital (first published in 1965).315

Lines of tendential force

Thus far, this chapter has taken several discrete steps. After recalling the enduring debate

surrounding the relationship between capital and ascriptive difference, it suggested the usefulness of

the language of articulation in our effort to make sense of the presence and persistence of logically

contingent patterns of racialization and gendered hierarchization in capitalist society. It turned to

Stuart Hall’s distinctive approach to the problem of the articulation of capital and difference—and

his reading of both Althusser and the modes of production controversy—suggesting that it

represents a particularly fertile and highly influential theorization in the present context. Indeed, my

contention, if it is not already entirely clear, is that Hall’s account—while generally focused on the

problem of race and racialization—represents perhaps the most critical effort to theorize the

articulation of racialized and gendered difference in capitalist society, insofar as it allows us to

demonstrate: (1) the relative autonomy of those phenomena and their structuring force across all

levels or instances of the social totality; (2) their determination in the last instance by “material

production and its relations,” relations that are themselves profoundly shaped by patterns of

racialized and gendered hierarchization368; and (3) the potentiality for race and gender to be re-

articulated in relation to the complex topography of the social whole, and remade into new forms of

racism and sexism over time. While gender is hardly one of the primary considerations in Hall’s

writing on the problem of articulation, my contention is that Hall’s analysis speaks to a range of

forms of ascriptive difference and hierarchization, not least gendered differentiation as well.

And yet, as clarifying as this account might be as a means of describing the contingent

association of capital and ascriptive difference within capitalist society, it seems to me that more

than a few open questions remain in light of this theorization. With Hall’s landmark account in view,

Nicos Poulantzas, the built environment, and state space

To this point, this chapter has made two moves. First, I established the conceptual history of

“articulation,” sketching its movement from Althusser to Hall, and underscoring its usefulness in the

context of contemporary debates on the relationship between capital and ascriptive difference.

Second, I developed a sympathetic critique of Hall’s highly influential and enduring account of the

articulation of capital and ascriptive hierarchization, highlighting the role of the built environment as

a modality of articulation and line of tendential force. Now, I will engage the problem of the

capitalist state to demonstrate how it is implicated in the spatial condensation and articulation of

capital’s constituent dynamics and contingent forms of racialized and gendered difference. To

engage this final problematic, I will return to the sociologist and state theorist Nicos Poulantzas and

his account of the capitalist state and state space.

articulation, the built environment, and the state: (1) the capitalist state is shaped by and shaping of

all kinds of relations and struggles within capitalist society, including struggles around capitalist

durability which informs the reproduction and continuity of capitalist society in general, not least as

a result of its “specific materiality” and spatial constitution; (3) the capitalist state informs the

production of, and is spatialized through, the fixity of the built environment; and (4) the capitalist

state, given its materialization in and through the built environment, is central to the spatialized

articulation of race, gender, and capital, and to their enduring articulation over time.

scholarship that the extended urban fabric is “not simply a product of state spatial strategies, but

serves as an important infrastructural scaffolding, medium, and expression of state power…as it is

Conclusion

This chapter has taken up a very specific relation to the concept of articulation. While some

scholars writing in the wake of Althusser have suggested that “[t]he social is articulation insofar as

‘society’ is impossible”—that articulation is a necessary feature of capitalist society precisely because

“there is no identity which can be fully constituted”—I have argued something rather different.470 I

have suggested that capitalist society is constituted by both necessary and contingent elements, with

race and gender falling squarely into the latter category. And I have insisted that in order to properly

grasp how the articulation and reproduction of these necessary and contingent elements takes place,

we must attend to the built environment. In the language of this dissertation, we must attend to the

role of the capitalist spatial matrix—intermeshed with and produced through the capitalist state—in

mediating the combination and condensation of these relations, and in shaping how the putatively

“raw materials [of] prior interpellations” are remade in the context of subsequent historical epochs

contingent parts, with a particular emphasis on its role in the reproduction of racialized and gendered

forms of hierarchization in that context.
