## Interpellation

In this final chapter of Part I, I will fill what remains a lacuna in my theorization of the role

of the built environment in the reproduction of capitalist society. I will consider how the production

of subjectivity and agency fits into the story told thus far; or, how the capitalist spatial matrix is

implicated in the production of historically contingent and differentiated forms of subjectivity and

the making of the uneven capacity for social action in capitalist contexts. After all, I have thus far

insisted that capitalist society is comprised of both foreground and background relations—and of

both logically necessary and logically contingent parts—which are subject to periodic re-

spatialization, re-articulation, and re-combination in and through the remaking of the built

environment. We might thus reasonably wonder how exactly that process of transformation and

social struggle takes place, and how the capacity for involvement in it is constituted in the first

instance. We might wonder how subjectivity and agency are both constituted and constrained. And

in this chapter, I will not only attempt to provide an answer to that question, partial as it will

necessarily be. But I will also insist that to properly grasp the production of subjectivity and the

constitution of agency in capitalist contexts, we must turn once again to the built environment. We

must turn squarely to the capitalist spatial matrix’s place in the production of historically contingent

forms of subjectification and in the constitution of differentiated forms of agency.

There are few questions more vexing in social-theoretical analysis than the one implied

above. In a sense, I have set for myself the task of engaging a particular manifestation of the

structure/agency problematic. Posing a version of this longstanding question in the present might

appear as passé. We are now, after all, some sixty years on from the infamous invitation of Jacques

Derrida to reject the dream of “full presence” and the ontotheology of “man and humanism”472; or,

beyond those infamous “postmodern” provocations, which sparked so much debate on the nature

Spaces of interpellation: Althusser and Fanon

As suggested above, a central aim of this chapter is to establish the role of the built

environment in the constitution and constraint of differentiated forms of capitalist subjectivity, with

the account developed in the preceding chapters in view. And, in that context, it is my contention

that we would do well to begin by turning to the concept of interpellation as it is developed in the

work of both Althusser and Fanon. Starting from Althusser is quite a natural choice. He is the single

figure most readily associated with the concept of interpellation, and its subsequent uptake in

materialist accounts of subjectification. Althusser develops his understanding of interpellation—

albeit in an elliptical and abbreviated form—in his widely read article “Ideology and Ideological State

Apparatuses (Notes Towards an Investigation).” That text was first published in French in 1970. It

was extracted from a longer manuscript that came to be posthumously published as Sur la

interpellation as part of a larger investigation into the reproduction of the relations of production.

Interpellation emerges in that text as central to his effort to make sense of how capitalist

reproduction takes place through the everyday actions of both workers and bosses alike—and

through their active participation in an iterative process of institutionally-mediated subjectification.487

There is a certain complexity—even ambiguity—to Althusser’s account in that text. He

argues that capitalist reproduction is primarily “secured” in and through the “exercise of state

trade unions, the media, and much more. What is most critical for our purposes, however, is that in

developing this argument, Althusser insists that these latter apparatuses operate not by violence but

through something resembling “consent,” even if that term “is conspicuously absent from the essay

and from Althusser’s work in general.” Althusser suggests, in other words, that the reproduction of

the relations of production occurs in capitalist contexts largely, if not exclusively, through

And yet, what is perhaps most important for our purposes is not only that Fanon is attentive

it becomes clear that interpellation is not simply the process through which subjects live

differentiated ideologies in distinctive geographies. We come to see, rather, that interpellation

presupposes and reproduces the built environment, which materializes and concretizes all of those

aspects that define capitalism as a complexly structured social whole—ideology, political power, economic

relations, and beyond. Indeed, in these classic works, we learn that subjects reproduce ideology in space

in and through their subjectification; and, more completely, that all of those dimensions that define

capitalist society as a totality—political power, economic relations, ideologies and norms—are

materialized and reproduced spatially via the actions of subjects and the built environment as well.

The built environment appears in these texts as produced by and productive of political, economic,

and ideological practices and norms—of the overdetermined capitalist socio-spatial totality—and as

integral to the production and reproduction of spatially differentiated subjectivities.

To clarify this argument, we can turn first to The Wretched of the Earth. In that text Fanon

The geography of history: Fanon, Hegel, and Sartre

My argument is that our reading of Althusser and Fanon does not leave us doomed to accept

the so-called “imperialism of the social object,” as Giddens might have it. In fact, Fanon himself

provides a critical resource in our engagement with these questions. To demonstrate this point, we

must simply turn not to Fanon’s above-sketched account of interpellation and subjectification, but

to his engagement with the philosophy of history. We must turn to the particular way in which

Fanon recasts Hegel’s teleology.549 And yet, to do so, I should first underscore what precisely I have

in view when referring to Hegel’s teleology. Here, I am referring—in abbreviated terms and broad

What we see by way of Fanon’s departure from Hegel is that while we are indeed all subject

differentiated forms of interpellation and subjectification?

My arguments in this and the preceding section are complex. But what I have established

above are several interrelated points, which can be stated directly. First, I have suggested that

interpellation and subjectification are not simply ideological processes that shape already existing

human subjectivities from the outside. They are socio-spatial processes, and our differentiated

interpellation and subjectification happens in and through our socio-spatial relations. We live our

differentiated subjectification in and through the built environment, which is the presupposition and

result of political, economic, and ideological relations. Second, I have argued that while all of this is

true, we still maintain the potentiality for forms of political action that exceed the parodic, and which

are capable of initiating a reweaving of the built environment itself. I have argued that we are the stuff

of freedom, which means that we have the capacity to reject and transform our “factical situations.”

## The “black belt”

Throughout the 1920s and 1930s a debate occupied some of the core theorists of American

communism. The “black belt debate,” as it came to be known, considered whether African

Americans in the post-Reconstruction south constituted an oppressed nation within the borders of the

United States. The debate largely took shape within the Communist Party of the United States of

America (CPUSA), and its proponents suggested that the so-called black belt—or “the soil

stretching from East Texas to Virginia, with its heartland in the prairies of Alabama and

Mississippi”—was not only an oppressed black nation, but a nation “which had the right to demand

self-determination.”628 This position reached its popular zenith in the early 1930s, following a series of

resolutions adopted by the Third International, which recognized “Negroes in the ‘black belt’

counties of the American South” in precisely those terms.629 Of course, the black belt debate was

largely waged in theory. The emergence of an autonomous black nation in the US south was never

practically in view. And yet, even if its material implications were indirect, the black belt debate

stands, at least for our purposes, as a critically revealing episode in the history of American political

economic thought. From its intellectual emergence via the ideals of Lenin in the 1910s630; to its

consolidation as an official party line in the late 1920s and early 1930s; to its formal abandonment in

1935 by the CPUSA, in its effort to “build a ‘popular front’ against fascism”631; the black belt debate

has much to teach us.

Indeed, in what follows I will take a first step in concretizing our theory of the role of the built

environment in the reproduction of capitalist society by attending to the black belt debate

specifically. I am not the first to turn to this historical episode with lofty ambitions. But while others

have engaged the black belt debate to think through the freedom dreams of the black radical

tradition or to consider the promises and pitfalls of identity politics in the present, my contention is

rather distinct. My claim is not only that the black belt debate represents a fascinating if

anachronistic attempt to think through the trajectory of political and economic life in the decades

immediately following the failures of Reconstruction. But, moreover, that the debate itself laid bare

the role of the built environment in the production and resolution of capitalist crises—and its role in

the reproduction of capital’s constituent parts. The thinkers implicated in the black belt debate did not

position their thought in this way. The black belt debate emerged in a different “problem-space,” to

use the language of David Scott, or in response to a different set of “historically situated questions”

for which only an historically situated set of answers was available.632 Nevertheless, in rereading the

black belt debate, we can concretize the role of the built environment in mediating those constitutive

crisis tendencies that structure capitalism as an institutionalized social order, and its role in resolving

crises that emerge across capitalism’s constitutive foreground and background abodes. Through the

black belt debate, we can further clarify our account of the role of the built environment in the

reproduction of capitalist society at the highest level of conceptual abstraction.

In the pages that follow I will attend to the oeuvre produced by key participants in the black

belt debate throughout the 1930s, and to the work of CPUSA members James S. Allen and Harry

Lenin, the Comintern, and the survivals of slavery

Before proceeding, we would do well to situate the black belt debate within its intellectual-

historical context, and to outline its primary contours and political and theoretical stakes. In the first

instance, we would do well to recall that the black belt thesis was adopted by the CPUSA in the late

1920s, in no small part because of the intellectual and political concerns of Lenin, which well

predated the thesis’ entry into US political debate. Lenin was long interested in the condition of

African Americans and with the enduring “survivals of slavery” (as he put it) in the US south

following the American Civil War. In 1913, Lenin drafted his first text on that subject. It was a short

article titled “Russians and Negroes”—and it was not published until 1925 in Krasnaya Niva,

following his death—but it represented a clear effort to think through the “feudal remnants” that

structured the Russian social formation of his time by way of a consideration of the enduring

survivals of slavery in the American south. He continued to develop these comparative concerns

throughout the 1910s. In 1915 Lenin published “Capitalism and Agriculture in the United States of

America,” which broadly considered the encroachment of capitalist forms of life and development

in agriculture across the United States, and which returned several times to the specific case of post-


<!-- Page 210 -->

service system,” and as one which left even ostensibly “emancipated” African Americans “hemmed in,

isolated and deprived of fresh air.”633 Indeed, even in 1917 Lenin made time to draft a text titled

“Statistics and Sociology,” which dealt again with African American life, feudal remnants, and

agrarian conditions in the south more specifically.634

In other words, throughout the 1910s the problem of African American oppression and its

relation to putatively non-capitalist forms of domination was, for Lenin, a central intellectual

concern. But the political stakes of this engagement only truly emerged in 1920. After several years of

As stated at several points in this chapter, my argument is not that participants in the black

belt debate were consciously engaged in theorizing the spatiality of capitalist reproduction. Figures

like Allen and Haywood were not consciously attuned to how crises of capitalist reproduction

emerged across capitalism’s foreground and background spheres, nor were they centrally concerned

with how crises were resolved in and through transformations in the built environment. And yet, we

can nonetheless identify these dynamics in their accounts of the post-Reconstruction black belt. We

Conclusion

This chapter has developed a single argument. It has suggested that the black belt debate—

taken as a critical moment in the history of heterodox political economic thought and anti-imperial

politics in the United States—provides an archive of thinking on the spatiality of capitalist crisis.

Key participants in the black belt debate were centrally concerned not simply with the politics of

black self-determination in the US south, nor even with the relationship between waged labor and

capitalist crisis. They were concerned, more capaciously, with tracking the constitutive crisis

tendencies of capital across its foreground and background abodes, and the concurrent re-

spatialization of the capitalist spatial matrix. Of course, Allen and Haywood would have described

their work in radically different terms. But insofar as they attempted to make sense of the political

economic, political-ecological, and reproductive regimes that emerged in the aftermath of

Reconstruction, they engaged with striking consistency—if not necessarily analytical clarity—the

spatiality of capitalist crisis and its relation to the built environment at a high level of conceptual

abstraction. And in turning finally to the work of figures like James Boggs and Huey Newton, I have

suggested—albeit briefly—that the colonial analytic continued to provide a window onto the

spatiality of capitalist crisis in the decades that followed the black belt debate. These later figures

deployed the language of colonialism in ways that called attention to the role of the built

environment in the reproduction of capital’s constituent crisis dynamics. They attended—in their

own terms—to the recurrent and endemic re-spatialization of capitalist society’s constitutive hidden

abodes.

## The “social factory”

In the context of the domestic labor debate of the 1970s and 1980s, Silvia Federici and

Angela Davis would seem to share little in common. After all, the domestic labor debate revolved

around the question of whether or not “households were sites of production with labor

processes…that produced value for capital”—and whether or not capital could be reproduced

without unwaged domestic work.761 In relation to that question, Federici and Davis pursued distinct,

indeed divergent, positions. Federici—who immigrated to the United States via Italy in 1967 and

founded the New York Wages for Housework Campaign in the early 1970s—approached the

problem of housework with the tradition of Italian operaismo (workerism) in view. She followed

Mario Tronti’s landmark claim in Workers and Capital (first published as Operai e capitale in 1966) that

at its most advanced level of development, all capitalist social relations stand as “moment[s] of the

relation of production”; that “society becomes an articulation of production, the whole society lives in

function of the factory and the factory extends its exclusive dominion over the whole society.”762

And she extended that argument. She argued that capital had always “mystified the social function of

the family” and gendered domestic work, and obscured the “subordination of all social relations to

the ‘cash nexus.’”763 Federici insisted that the wage form did not simply rely on relations of

production beyond the factory in the context of advanced capitalism, but that it obscured the

requisite work of social reproduction that took place within the home in all capitalist contexts. The

“numerically small class,” according to Inman, helped to instantiate the legal oppression of women

under feudal systems and to “bind[] [them] anew to subjugation” with the emergence of capitalism.

The prison and the ghetto: geographies of articulation

As briefly noted above, it is not entirely novel to suggest that spatiality was a concern within

the US iteration of the domestic labor debate. Some figures, like the architectural historian and

urbanist Dolores Hayden—discussed in more depth below—organized their engagement with that

debate in explicitly and exclusively spatial terms. Across a series of articles and books, Hayden

attempted to sketch the parameters of what she called a “non-sexist city”—to develop “a new

relation of women to that domain—contributed to the production of womanhood as well. Even

appeared in a variety of guises—women’s “isolation within the four walls of the house, isolation of

waged workers in relation to houseworkers, isolation of daycare activists from one neighbourhood

to another.”826 Some even argued that “woman” was “crystallized” in and through this pattern of

spatial isolation.827

In what follows below I will extend this observation—regarding the place of spatiality in the

domestic labor debate—along two conceptual axes. First, I will take up a reading of invocations of

the “prison” and the “ghetto” by Angela Davis specifically, arguing that in her consideration of

those spatial categories, she helped to clarify the role of the built environment in the articulation of

ascriptive difference and the constituent features of capitalist society. I will argue that Davis

demonstrated, more specifically, that “gender” did not exist in isolation or in the abstract, but was

always differentially enacted via the built environment and articulated in an overdetermined socio-

spatial whole. And second, I will suggest that we can read invocations of the “household” and the

“suburb”—in the work of Silvia Federici and Dolores Hayden, respectively—to grasp the

constitutive spatiality of differentiated patterns of interpellation, or the role of the built environment in

the interpellation of social subjects and the depth of their interior lives. In other words, I will not

only highlight the presence of spatial categories and concepts across the domestic labor debate.

Rather, I will draw attention to the invocation of specific categories related to the built environment

in light of this dissertation’s broad problematic. I will demonstrate that in and through their

engagement with these four spatial categories—the prison, the ghetto, the household, and the

suburb—a disparate and often divergent array of thinkers associated with the domestic labor debate

brought the role of the built environment in the reproduction of capitalist society—in all of its

complexity—into view.

those figures associated with the domestic labor debate, was unsurprisingly the most attuned to the

spatiality and material architecture of the prison. Her personal experience of imprisonment—which

followed from her involvement in the defense of the Soledad Brothers and her arrest in 1970—

loomed large in her writing. The steel bars, the “white tile walls and light-colored linoleum floor[s],”

The household and the suburb: geographies of interpellation

In the preceding section I provided an argument regarding the relationship between the built

environment and the articulation of race, gender, and capital. My concern was not with how space

becomes racialized and gendered per se. It was not with the so-called “norming of space and the

person” via the ideological norming of space and the imprinting of individuals with the

“characteristics of a certain kind of space,” and vice versa.867 Rather, what I attempted to

demonstrate was that particular forms of ascriptive identity—which are logically contingent to the

functional reproduction of capital—are articulated within the capitalist socio-spatial whole via their

enactment in the built environment. Ascriptive identities do not precede their overdetermined

Conclusion

While the previous chapter turned to the history of the black belt debate to give shape to our

theorization of the role of the built environment in the production and resolution of capitalist crises,

in this chapter I have attempted to further substantiate my claim that the built environment has a

central role to play in both the processes of articulation and interpellation. What I have argued is

that, despite the disagreements that constituted the US iteration of the domestic labor debate in the

1970s and 1980s, several key participants within that debate invoked spatial categories to develop

their arguments, revealing crucial insights in the present context. In the work of Angela Davis, we

see clearly that gender itself is not static or stable, but always overdetermined, enacted, and

articulated in the context of a broader socio-spatial whole and via the built environment; and in the

work of Silvia Federici and Dolores Hayden we see that the built environment is implicated in the

process of subjectification in the most intimate sense—in the construction of a “lifeworld,” and a

sense of “the way things are and will be.”908 In other words, in each of these thinkers the built

environment appears as central not simply to the reproduction of capital’s constitutive features, but

to capitalist society—to its necessary and contingent parts.

## Conclusion

While the long history of political and social thought has given relatively short shrift to the

built environment—albeit with a few notable exceptions, particularly since the 1970s—the built

environment itself is hardly absent in contemporary political debate. We find it at the center of many

of the pressing political questions of the day, whether or not it is framed in precisely that way.

Commentators writing about the green transition, to name but one area of political concern, often

note that “we are not starting from scratch”—and that we must grapple with the existing built

environment.909 Within the scholarship in that broad domain, it is well understood that the fossil

economy emerged in tandem with a particular kind of built environment, or—as Adam Hanieh has

recently put it—“a specific form of urbanism – high density and energy intensive towns and cities,

filled with concentrated areas of residential and industrial facilities powered by fossil fuels”910; and,

moreover, that each subsequent era in the development of the fossil economy required its own built

environment, which was layered atop the preceding strata of built space. For contemporary political

commentators this simple fact contributes to the complexity of the politics of “asset stranding,” and

to the complexity of the move away from fossil fuels. The stranding of existing fossil fuel

infrastructure will necessarily implicate not just a few nodal points within an interconnected

geography, but the entire built landscape which “imparts inertia to capital.”911 “Over the living,” the

909 Brett Christophers, The Price is Wrong: Why Capitalism Won’t Save the Planet (New York: Verso, 2024), 156. 910 Adam Hanieh, Crude Capitalism: Oil, Corporate Power, and the Making of the World Market (New York: Verso, 2024), 18. 911 Andreas Malm and Wim Carton, Overshoot: How the World Surrendered to Climate Breakdown (New York: Verso, 2024), 107.


<!-- Page 286 -->


276

dead labor embedded in the built environment constitutes “a mute and stifling power” that will have

to be engaged if we are to move beyond fossil fuels.912

This kind of critical engagement with the built environment is welcome, as are the

comparable and overlapping discussions that take place on themes like housing, transportation,

segregation, and the like. In the face of the crises of the present, we will undoubtedly have to grapple

with the contours of the really existing built environment, and engage its pertinence within several

specified policy domains. Nevertheless, this kind of political engagement with the built environment

admittedly sits somewhat awkwardly in relation to the theorization that I have developed throughout

this dissertation. After all, across the preceding pages, I have made sense of the built environment in

terms that are both broader and more abstract than even the most capacious engagements with that

topic in the realm of policy and politics today. Rather than attending to policy-oriented debates on

the fossil economy, housing, segregation, or any other domain, I have taken the critical literature on

capitalist reproduction as my primary intellectual foil, rejecting its tendencies toward

“obscurantism,” “essentialism,” and “reductionism.” I have emphasized that it is through the built

environment—or through that relatively fixed and immobile environment that surrounds us, and

that preempts particular forms of use—that capitalist society’s necessary and contingent dynamics

are materialized, concretized, and reproduced. Indeed, by way of a reading of the history of

heterodox political economic thought in the United States, I have argued that the built environment

mediates capitalism’s inherent and recurrent crises, articulates capitalist society’s necessary and

contingent relations, and interpellates historically differentiated capitalist subjects. I have positioned

the built environment not as a site of policy intervention per se, but as a key moment in the

reproduction of capitalist society in its conjunctural specificity and complexity.

912 Malm and Carton, Overshoot, 219.


<!-- Page 287 -->


277

Of course, the political implications of this account have not gone entirely unaddressed. In

my theorization of the capitalist spatial matrix, I have done my best not to “bestow a cohesiveness”

upon it which it “utterly lacks.”913 I have emphasized that the built environment in capitalist contexts

is open to contestation, remaking, and change. I have also suggested that this general account of the

built environment is necessary if we are to address some of the most pressing and politically-

contested debates within contemporary social thought, not least those surrounding the relationship

between capitalism and ascriptive differentiation—on “racial capitalism,” “patriarchal capitalism,”

“class abstractionism,” and beyond. Given that those debates often turn on an unstated and

unengaged disagreement regarding the constitutive relations of capitalist society and regarding how

and why those relations relate to forms of ascriptive differentiation, my theorization of the capitalist

spatial matrix has much to recommend in that context. With the preceding chapters in view, we are

well positioned to identify the constitutive dynamics that define capitalist society, and to explicate

their reproduction in and through space. We are also well positioned to consider how and why

capitalist society comes to be racialized and gendered, why it remains so over time, and how exactly

the articulation of race, gender, and capital might be struggled against. With that said, we are,

nonetheless, still quite far from the concrete questions that animate contemporary engagements with

the built environment within the realm of policy and politics today. Not only does my account sit

awkwardly in relation to debates on, inter alia, fossil fuel infrastructure, transportation, housing,

segregation, and the like, but one might reasonably wonder how my account sheds light on those

concrete matters of concern at all. How does this dissertation speak to concrete concerns regarding

the politics of the built environment?

913 Lefebvre, The Production of Space, 11.


<!-- Page 288 -->


278

In response to such a question, my concluding claim is not that the arguments of this

dissertation provide a straightforward path forward, much less a practical guide to policy making

regarding the built environment in the present. In fact, my claim is just the opposite. What follows

from the preceding pages is not a concrete political agenda, but the observation that any discussion

of the built environment is but a window into a much broader set of ethical and normative considerations that

must be engaged. Throughout this dissertation, I have suggested that the built environment is at the

core of the reproduction of capitalist society, in spite of the fact that it has been relatively

overlooked in the long history of political and social thought, and generally misapprehended by the

post-1970s traditions of radical geography and critical socio-spatial theory. And what follows from

my core claims is that what we imagine and what we struggle for is always conditioned by the built

environment in capitalist contexts; that the built environment itself contains the trace of our

freedom or the “movement of transcendence.”914 Indeed, the built environment is the “given,” as

Simone de Beauvoir puts it, that defines our freedom and that must be remade in our movement

toward the future.915 How we choose to live and reproduce our built environment will shape the

forms of economic life we will have, the processes of hierarchization that will (or will not) define

our society, and the kinds of subjectivities that we will be. In reproducing the capitalist built

environment, we not only reproduce our economic system, but life more generally; we produce

conditions that “allow, afford, encourage, permit, suggest, [and] influence” certain kinds of life, and

inhibit others.916

914 Sartre, Critique of Dialectical Reason, Volume One, 236. 915 Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity (New York: Citadel Press, 1976). 916 Cf. Latour, Reassembling the Social, 72.


<!-- Page 289 -->


279

The built environment is integral to the reproduction of—as Manuel Castells put it—the

“specific laws regarding the conversion of capitalist social relationships.”917 But it is also much more

than the materialization of capital’s laws. It is the medium through which the necessary and

contingent relations of capitalist society are concretized and condensed. And as such, any

engagement with the built environment entails a decision regarding what we want to maintain and

what we want to transcend. The political or normative lesson of this dissertation is that any

engagement with the built environment raises the question of what we are struggling against, and what

we are struggling for.
